Series::hardswish¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::hardswish() const
Series& Series::hardswish_() const

A Bounded Gate With A Linear Positive Tail¶

hardswish() transforms every element with the piecewise function

                 0                    when x <= -3
hardswish(x) =   x * (x + 3) / 6      when -3 < x < 3
                 x                    when x >= 3

The method combines a value with a cheap, bounded gate. Large negative values are suppressed, large positive values pass through unchanged, and values in the transition interval are attenuated by a quadratic curve. Use it when that specific activation contract is useful. Use hardsigmoid() when the gate itself, rather than the gated value, is the desired result.

The operation is elementwise: rank, shape, element order, and platform are preserved. It allocates a new contiguous result and does not mutate the receiver. Floating receivers retain their dtype. Integral and Boolean receivers are promoted to float32, because the middle branch generally contains fractions. Complex receivers are rejected: the branch tests require an ordered real value.

The endpoint choices are deliberate. x == -3 belongs to the zero branch and x == 3 belongs to the identity branch. Those choices also determine the one-sided reverse rule at the two corners.

Reverse Mode¶

For a tracked floating receiver, the recorded derivative is

                  0                 when x <= -3
d/dx hardswish =  (2x + 3) / 6      when -3 < x < 3
                  1                 when x >= 3

The interior derivative depends on x, so higher-order differentiation can observe nonzero curvature inside the transition interval. At -3 the selected derivative is 0; at 3 it is 1.

In-Place Form¶

hardswish_() is the in-place sibling of hardswish(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — hardswish_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-4.0, 0.0, 4.0});
x.hardswish_();
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 4]

Examples¶

Example 1. The boundary values show all three branches.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-4.0, -3.0, -1.5, 0.0, 1.5, 3.0, 4.0})
        .hardswish());

Output¶

Series(shape=[7], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=7, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.0000, -0.3750, 0.0000, 1.1250, 3.0000, 4.0000]

Example 2. Higher-rank integer input keeps its shape and promotes to float32 before fractional values are formed.

auto y = pluss::make_series({{-4, -2, 0}, {1, 3, 4}}).hardswish();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, y);
std::cout << "dtype=" << y.scalar_type()
          << " dim=" << y.dim()
          << " shape=[" << y.size(0) << ',' << y.size(1) << ']';

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 0.0000 -0.3333 0.0000 ⎤
⎣ 0.6667  3.0000 4.0000 ⎦
dtype=float32 dim=2 shape=[2,3]

Example 3. Summing the output exposes the endpoint and interior derivatives.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-4.0, -3.0, -1.5, 0.0, 1.5, 3.0, 4.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.hardswish().sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[7], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=7, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 0.5000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000]

Example 4. The result can act as a value-dependent gate in a larger elementwise expression.

auto payload = pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 30.0});
auto control = pluss::make_series({-4.0, 0.0, 4.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, payload.mul(control.hardswish()));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.0000, 120.0000]

Example 5. Complex values have no ordering for the branch boundaries.

try {
  using Complex = std::complex<double>;
  (void)pluss::make_series(std::vector<Complex>{{1.0, 1.0}}, {1})
      .hardswish();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  const std::string message = e.what();
  std::cout << message.substr(0, message.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

hardswish: complex input is not supported

See Also¶

  • hardsigmoid() returns the bounded gate without multiplying by the receiver.

  • mish() is a smooth activation without piecewise corners.

  • relu() suppresses negative values without a transition interval.
